On the screen. Open the Tonga page, download the 2021 report in front of the room, and search the PDF for the word remittance so they watch the figure appear.

Say why this demonstration is the important one. Every other source on today's list counts money crossing a border. This is the only one that counts households, and the question your assignment asks, which is who receives and who decides, cannot begin without it.

Remind the room of the slide on three surveys earlier today. What this report tells you depends entirely on what the survey asked. Tonga’s 2021 survey asked one question about cash in the last twelve months and found 90 in every hundred households. The 2004 research survey asked about goods, school fees and bills paid as well, and also found 90 in every hundred, at a time when the national survey asking the narrow question found 75. So copy the question wording into your notes, not just the number, because the next person who reads your work will need it.

Read the breakdowns aloud, because they are where the module’s argument lives. In Tonga 96 in every hundred households headed by a woman received cash against 88 headed by a man, and 94 in Vava’u against 64 in Ongo Niua. The national figure of 90 hides both of those.

Then deal with the honest case. Many islands have no recent survey, or a survey whose report does not give this figure. Tell the students plainly that writing “not found, and here is where I looked” scores higher than a number they cannot source, and that the Microdata Library is the place to look next because it holds the questionnaires even where the data is closed.

If a link is dead on the day. Search for your country’s name with the words household income and expenditure survey report, or living conditions survey, and look for the statistics office’s own domain, which usually ends in gov. The office is also often called the bureau of statistics or, in French, l’institut national de la statistique.

For an island we have not covered. The survey has four common names: household income and expenditure survey, living conditions survey, household budget survey, and integrated household survey. Try all four. If nothing comes back, the regional body often holds it: the Pacific Community for Pacific islands, CARICOM for the Caribbean, and the World Bank Microdata Library for everywhere.

Part one · Where to find the figures · Demonstration 7 of 8

The lender’s own project documents are the only place that says who a project was meant to reach and how many it reached

The question this answers: behind one line of the aid total, who was the money for?

The project list for Jamaica on projects.worldbank.org
World Bank projects, JamaicaWorld Bank projects, all countriesAsian Development Bank projectsInter-American Development Bank projects
The clicks, in order
  1. Open projects.worldbank.org and click the Project List tab.
  2. Open Country in the filter panel on the left, choose your country and click Go. The address then carries your country code, so you can change it directly next time.
  3. The table gives the project title, the identifier beginning with P, the commitment amount, the status and the approval date. Open a project whose title looks relevant to a livelihood: housing, social protection, water, schools.
  4. Inside the project, click the Documents tab.
  5. Open the Project Appraisal Document, written before the money is spent. It states who the project is for and how many people it should reach.
  6. Open the Implementation Completion Report, written afterwards, which says how many it actually reached. For a project funded elsewhere, the Asian Development Bank and the Inter-American Development Bank publish the same two documents.
What you should see

Jamaica has 161 World Bank projects listed. The most recent is the Hurricane Melissa Reconstruction Implementation Support Project, P515022, five million US dollars, approved 30 June 2026.

Tonga’s largest current project is the Sustainable Economic Corridors and Urban Resilience Project, P512750: an 80 million US dollar grant from the Asian Development Bank, a 40 million World Bank grant and 25 million from the Government of Tonga, for a bridge across the Fanga’uta lagoon with roads and drainage in Nuku’alofa.

This is the bridge into part two of today. The appraisal document is the only document in the whole day that names a target group, and even it names a number of people rather than a household.

What this source cannot tell you. Whether the people named as the target were the people reached. The completion report gives a count, and no document here follows a single household.

Sources

World Bank. (n.d.). Projects & Operations. Retrieved September 18, 2026, from https://projects.worldbank.org/

Asian Development Bank. (n.d.). Projects. Retrieved September 18, 2026, from https://www.adb.org/projects

On the screen. Open the Jamaica project list, open the Hurricane Melissa reconstruction project, and go straight to the Documents tab so the room sees the appraisal document and the completion report sitting side by side.

Explain what these two documents are, because most students have never seen one. Before a lender releases money it writes an appraisal document, which argues why the project is needed, states who it is for, and commits to a number of people it will reach. Years later it writes a completion report, which says what happened. Both are public, both are long, and almost nobody outside the institution reads them.

These are the only documents in today’s whole list that name a group of people. Every figure we have opened until now counts dollars crossing a border. Ask the room to hold that thought into part two, where the question becomes who decides.

Show them how to read one without reading all of it. The appraisal document has a results framework near the front, usually a table, giving the indicators and the target numbers. The completion report has the same table with the achieved column filled in. Those two tables are the five minutes of reading that matter.

Ask each group to find one project on its own island and to say, from the appraisal document, who the project names as its beneficiaries and whether a household like theirs would be among them.

If a link is dead on the day. Search World Bank projects and operations and use the Project List tab, then the Country filter. For the regional banks search Asian Development Bank projects or Inter-American Development Bank projects.

For an island we have not covered. Find out which bank lends to your island and go to that bank’s project pages. The Asian Development Bank covers the Pacific, the Inter-American Development Bank and the Caribbean Development Bank cover the Caribbean, and the African Development Bank covers the Indian Ocean and Atlantic islands. All four publish appraisal and completion documents under the same two names.

Part one · Where to find the figures · The method for any island

The three figures exist for every small island state, and the method for finding them is the same wherever your island is

The question this answers: what do you do when the island you are writing about is not Tonga, Jamaica or the Comoros?

The balance of payments page of the Banque Centrale des Comores, the thinnest of our three cases
World Bank Open Data, all indicatorsOECD Data ExplorerWorld Bank Microdata Library
The clicks, in order
  1. Aid, share of national income. One page on data.worldbank.org holds every country. Change the two letter code, or find your country in the table under the chart. This one never fails.
  2. Who paid. The OECD Data Explorer holds every aid recipient in the world, and the recipient filter behaves the same way for every island.
  3. Who paid that the OECD misses. The Non-DAC branch of the same table, plus AidData for China. Lowy only if your island is in the Pacific.
  4. Remittances. Every central bank publishes a balance of payments, because the IMF requires it. Search your country plus central bank and look for a menu called Statistics, Economic Reviews or Publications. The line may be called personal transfers, workers’ remittances, secondary income or transferts courants.
  5. Households. The survey goes by four names: household income and expenditure, living conditions, household budget, integrated household. Try all four, then the Microdata Library, then the regional body.
  6. When you find nothing. Write what you searched for, where you looked and on what date, and put that in your map in place of a number. An absence you can describe is evidence.
What you should see

Tonga in the Pacific and Jamaica in the Caribbean: every source on this list works for both. The Comoros in the Indian Ocean: three of the six are thin, and it still yields all three figures.

The Comoros is the case worth studying, because most islands resemble it. Its central bank spreadsheet stops in 2021 and uses an older edition of the IMF manual, and its largest donors are multilateral banks and Gulf governments rather than the countries a Pacific example teaches you to expect. It still has an aid share, a remittance share and a survey in the Microdata Library. Thin is not the same as absent.

What this source cannot tell you. Nothing, if you work through it in order. What no source will give you is who inside the household decided, which is why tomorrow you map it rather than look it up.

Sources

World Bank. (n.d.). World Bank Open Data. Retrieved September 18, 2026, from https://data.worldbank.org/

Banque Centrale des Comores. (2023, January 19). Statistiques de la balance des paiements. Retrieved September 18, 2026, from https://banque-comores.km/page/show/statistiques-de-la-balance-des-paiements

On the screen. Ask the room to call out an island that is not one of our three, then find its aid share and its remittance share live, in front of them, using only this slide. It takes about ninety seconds and it is the most convincing thing you can do all afternoon.

Say what the three worked cases are for. Tonga is the Pacific, Jamaica is the Caribbean, the Comoros is the Indian Ocean and it is also the data poor case. Between them they cover the three seas where small island developing states sit, and one example of what happens when the statistics office is under resourced. If the method works for those three it works for the rest.

The two sources that never fail are the World Bank indicator pages, because every country in the world is on them, and the OECD Data Explorer, because every aid recipient is in its recipient filter. Start there whatever your island.

The two that sometimes fail are the central bank and the household survey, and both fail in the same way: the material exists but it is old, or it is inside a PDF, or it is in French or Portuguese. Show them the Comoros page on the screen and read the line that says the spreadsheet runs from 2003 to 2021. That is not a dead end. It is a figure with a date, and a date is what the module asks for.

End on the rule that governs the classwork. Beside every figure, write what it measures, the year and where you found it. Where you found nothing, write what you searched for and when. A map that records its own gaps is worth more than a map with every cell filled in.

Part two

A dollar of aid and a dollar of remittance have the same value, but different people decide how each is used

The two flows arrive under different conditions, and the studies that have measured them together found that they have different effects. Tonga is the worked example.

Who decides

Aid passes through five decisions before it reaches a household. A remittance passes through one.

What studies find

Eight of the 201 studies in the FAR-SIDS review measured both flows at once, and two of them matter for islands.

Tonga in both accounts

The same country read from the national accounts, and then read from the household.

A dollar of aid and a dollar of remittance have the same value, and different people decide how each is spent. The two arrive under different conditions, and the studies that have measured them together found that they have different effects. Everything in the rest of the block depends on this observation, so the next slide makes it concrete by following each kind of money from the people who decide it to the household that receives it. Tonga, which receives both flows on a large scale, is the worked example throughout.

Part two · Who decides

Aid passes through five decisions before it reaches a household, whereas a remittance arrives with a named person

The shaded steps are where the household enters each chain. Aid decisions are written down and are made far from the household, whereas remittance decisions are made close to the household and are written down nowhere.

Ask the room

At which step of the aid chain does anybody ask the household what it needs? At which step of the remittance chain is anything written down that a ministry could read?

Sources

World Bank. (n.d.). Remittance Prices Worldwide: New Zealand to Tonga [Data set]. Retrieved September 17, 2026, from https://remittanceprices.worldbank.org/corridor/New-Zealand/Tonga

In the aid chain, a donor parliament, in Canberra, Wellington or Brussels, sets the aid budget, and the donor's aid agency sets the priorities, such as health in one year and roads in the next. Your government then negotiates the project and often contributes some of its own money, and the project team writes the selection rule that decides which villages and which households take part. Some households qualify and some do not, and the household that qualifies usually receives a service, such as a clinic, a water tank or a road, and rarely receives cash.

The remittance chain is shorter, because a family member abroad earns the money, the transfer company takes its fee, which on the World Bank's Remittance Prices Worldwide series was 7.89% from New Zealand to Tonga and 7.65% from Australia to Tonga in the third quarter of 2025, so about 8 dollars in every 100 sent, and the money arrives with one named person, such as a mother, a sister or a grandmother. The household then decides, inside the house, what to do with it. Ask the room at which step of the aid chain anybody asks the household what it needs. The usual answer is the fourth step at the earliest, and often none. Then ask at which step of the remittance chain anything is written down that a ministry could read, and the answer is none, apart from the transfer company's record of the amount. Thus aid decisions are recorded on paper and made far from the household, whereas remittance decisions are made inside the household and recorded nowhere.

Part two · What studies find when they measure both

Studies that measure aid and remittances together find that the two flows have different effects

Eight of the 201 studies in the FAR-SIDS systematic review put aid and remittances into the same statistical model. Two of those eight produced results that matter for islands.

The real exchange rateThe price of what your island produces compared with the price of the same goods abroad. When a lot of foreign money arrives at once, prices and wages at home rise, so a Tongan squash exporter or a hotel in Nuku'alofa becomes more expensive for a buyer in Auckland.
Dutch diseaseThe name economists give to that effect, after what happened in the Netherlands when income from natural gas arrived in the 1960s. Aid produced it across the nineteen islands and remittances did not, most likely because households spend remittances on food, school and housing rather than on large projects.
Sources

Amuedo-Dorantes, C., Pozo, S., & Vargas-Silva, C. (2007). Remittances and the macroeconomy: The case of small island developing states (WIDER Research Paper No. 2007/22). UNU-WIDER. https://www.wider.unu.edu/sites/default/files/rp2007-22.pdf

Werker, E., Ahmed, F. Z., & Cohen, C. (2009). How is foreign aid spent? Evidence from a natural experiment. American Economic Journal: Macroeconomics, 1(2), 225–244. https://doi.org/10.1257/mac.1.2.225

de Waegh, R. (2026). FAR-SIDS systematic review of aid, remittances and wellbeing in small island developing states [Unpublished review, 201 included studies]. Islands and Small States Institute, University of Malta.

The FAR-SIDS systematic review read 201 published studies on aid, remittances and wellbeing in small island states, and only eight of them put the two flows into the same statistical model, meaning that they measured both at once. Two of those eight produced results that matter for islands. The first result concerns the real exchange rate, which is the price of what your island produces compared with the price of the same goods abroad, and when a large amount of foreign money arrives at once, prices and wages at home rise, so a Tongan squash exporter or a hotel in Nuku'alofa becomes more expensive for a buyer in Auckland and sells less. Economists call this Dutch disease, after what happened in the Netherlands when income from natural gas arrived in the 1960s. Amuedo-Dorantes, Pozo and Vargas-Silva (2007) found across nineteen small island states that aid produced this effect and remittances did not, and the most likely reason is who spends the money, because aid is spent by governments and on large projects, whereas remittances are spent by households on food, school and housing.

The second result concerns spending: Werker, Ahmed and Cohen (2009) showed that when a study counts remittances, the measured effect of aid on consumption and imports falls by up to one third. Families were sending money at the same time as donors were giving aid, so the studies that left remittances out had attributed to aid what families were paying for. From this position, adding the two flows together into one figure would hide exactly the differences this module is about, which is why the module keeps them apart.

Part two · When a labour scheme produces remittances

Governments design the labour schemes that produce many Pacific remittances, yet the money is counted as private

20,750

places a year

New Zealand's Recognised Seasonal Employer scheme, capped at this number since August 2024.

3,715

Tongans on PALM visas

In Australia on 30 June 2026 under the Pacific Australia Labour Mobility scheme, 3,095 of them men. On the same day 798 Tongans held New Zealand seasonal work visas, 729 of them men; the New Zealand season peaks in March, when 1,311 held them.

1 in 5

working Tongan men

A journalist's estimate for the two schemes together (1News, 2 August 2026), shown here as an estimate.

Is the scheme aid?The scheme is aid only in part. For the New Zealand scheme the OECD counts the workers’ training as aid and excludes the cost of running the scheme, because the scheme is there to fill labour shortages in New Zealand. For the Australian scheme it counts the part the aid ministry pays for, and it states that migrants sending money home is not on its own enough to make a programme aid.
For tomorrowAsk which of your island's remittance flows exist because of a government policy. Tonga's central bank has counted seasonal earnings within remittances since 2014, and they reached a tenth of the total by 2025.
Sources

OECD Development Assistance Committee. (2023). ODA casebook on activities in the field of migration (DCD/DAC/STAT(2023)34/FINAL). OECD. https://one.oecd.org/document/DCD/DAC/STAT(2023)34/FINAL/en/pdf

New Zealand Government. (2024, August 14). RSE scheme revitalised and cap increased [Press release]. https://www.beehive.govt.nz/release/rse-scheme-revitalised-and-cap-increased

Department of Employment and Workplace Relations. (2026). PALM scheme data publication, June 2026 [Data set]. Pacific Australia Labour Mobility scheme. https://www.palmscheme.gov.au/

Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment. (2026). Migration data explorer: Visa holder population by nationality and visa type [Data set]. Retrieved September 17, 2026, from https://www.mbie.govt.nz/immigration-and-tourism/immigration/migration-research-and-evaluation/migration-data-explorer

1News. (2026, August 2). Seasonal work in NZ helping Tongans build businesses back home. https://www.1news.co.nz/2026/08/02/seasonal-work-in-nz-helping-tongans-build-businesses-back-home/

Labour schemes are where the two kinds of money meet. New Zealand's Recognised Seasonal Employer scheme, capped at 20,750 places a year since August 2024, and Australia's Pacific Australia Labour Mobility scheme, known as PALM, bring Pacific workers to seasonal jobs such as picking fruit and packing meat, and they produce a large remittance flow by design. On 30 June 2026, 3,715 Tongans held PALM visas in Australia, 3,095 of them men, and on the same day 798 Tongans held New Zealand seasonal work visas, 729 of them men; New Zealand's season peaks in March, when 1,311 Tongans held them (MBIE, 2026). Both figures count people holding a visa on one day, so they can stand side by side. A journalist estimates that the two schemes together employ about one in five working Tongan men, and the screen shows that figure as an estimate.

A donor government therefore designs a labour scheme, the scheme produces remittances, and the remittances are counted as private transfers. The OECD has ruled on both schemes in its casebook. For the New Zealand scheme it counts the workers’ training programme as aid and excludes the cost of running the scheme, because employers must first show that they cannot fill the job locally, so the scheme is there to fill labour shortages in New Zealand. For the Australian scheme it counts the part the aid ministry pays for, and it states that migrants sending money home is not on its own enough to make a programme aid (OECD DAC, 2023). Thus the schemes are immigration policy with a small aid component, and they produce a private flow that barely appears in the aid statistics of the country that designed them. For tomorrow, ask which of your island's remittance flows exist because of a government policy. Jamaica has its own example, the Overseas Employment Programme, which sends workers to Canada and the United States.

Part two · What the money pays for

Tongan households that received more remittances earned more from business, and Fijian households did not

A coefficientThe number a statistical model gives for how much one thing changes when another rises by one. Here, for every extra dollar of remittances a Tongan household received, its business income was on average 52 cents higher.
What it does not showThe result is an association measured at one point in time, and the authors state that it does not prove the dollar caused the business. They explain the difference between Tonga and Fiji by the age of the migration corridor.
Sources

Brown, R. P. C., & Leeves, G. (2011). Comparative effects of migrants’ remittances on composition of recipient household income in two small, island economies. Applied Economics, 43(27), 3965–3976. https://doi.org/10.1080/00036841003742611

Brown and Leeves, reading 2, asked the same questions in the same year in Tonga and in Fiji to find out what remittances pay for once they arrive. They report the answer as a coefficient, which is the number a statistical model gives for how much one thing changes when another rises by one. In Tonga the coefficient on business income was 0.52, which means that for every extra dollar of remittances a household received, its business income was on average 52 cents higher. In Fiji there was no such effect, and the only consistent result was lower wage income, meaning that people worked fewer paid hours (Brown and Leeves, 2011, Table 6).

The result is an association measured at one point in time, and the authors state that it does not prove the dollar caused the business. They explain the difference by the age of the migration corridor. Tongans have migrated regularly for four decades, so families can plan around the money and invest part of it, whereas migration from Fiji is more recent and the money arrives less predictably. For a ministry, this means that how long the money has been arriving and how regularly it comes matter as much as the amount.

Part two · What the money pays for

In rural Samoa, households spent 29 dollars of every 100 received from abroad on customary obligations and church giving

Fa'alavelaveThe Samoan term for customary obligations such as weddings, funerals, elections and titles. It took 17 dollars of every 100 received, before any ordinary spending.
MisinaleThe annual church donation in Tonga. About a third of remittance transactions are at least partly intended for it, and one study had to report household income twice, with and without those transfers.
KavengaThe Tongan term for obligation in general: the duties a household owes to kin, church and community. Meeting them maintains a household's standing and its right to call on others in a crisis.
What is not measuredNo published wellbeing indicator records this spending, and nobody has yet measured what share of Tongan household income goes to kavenga and misinale.
Sources

Le Dé, L., Gaillard, J. C., Friesen, W., & Matautia Smith, F. (2015). Remittances in the face of disasters: A case study of rural Samoa. Environment, Development and Sustainability, 17(3), 653–672. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10668-014-9559-0

McKenzie, D., Gibson, J., & Stillman, S. (2007). Moving to opportunity, leaving behind what? Evaluating the initial effects of a migration policy on incomes and poverty in source areas. New Zealand Economic Papers, 41(2), 197–223. https://doi.org/10.1080/00779950709558509

Le Dé and colleagues, reading 4, found that in rural Samoa before the 2009 tsunami the largest single use of remittances was neither food nor housing. Households spent about 17 dollars of every 100 received on fa'alavelave, the customary obligations of weddings, funerals, elections and titles, and about 12 dollars on church donations, so 29 dollars of every 100 went to obligations before any ordinary spending, while small business received 3 (Le Dé et al., 2015, p. 664). In Tonga the annual church donation is the misinale, and about a third of remittance transactions are at least partly intended for it, so one study had to report household income twice, once with those transfers and once without them (McKenzie, Gibson and Stillman, 2007, p. 207). Kavenga is the Tongan term for obligation in general, meaning the duties a household owes to kin, church and community. Ask the room for the word on their own island, because most islands have one.

This spending should not be read as waste, because kavenga and misinale maintain a household's standing and its right to call on others when something goes wrong, and in a country with almost no formal insurance, that standing is what a household relies on in a crisis. However, the spending is invisible in the official figures, because no published wellbeing indicator records it and nobody has yet measured what share of Tongan household income goes to it. A household survey could measure it, and we return to that possibility in part three.

Part two · What the migrant no longer contributes

A household with a migrant gains the remittances and loses the migrant's work at home, and many calculations count only the gain

The simple methodTake the household's income, subtract the remittances, and call the difference the gain from migration. The method assumes that the person who left would have earned nothing at home.
The counterfactualThe economists' term for what would have happened otherwise: what the migrant would have earned, grown and cared for if they had stayed. Once it is counted, the measured fall in poverty in Latin America shrinks from 14% to 3%.
A migration lottery as evidenceNew Zealand ran a ballot for Tongan migration, so chance decided who left. The families who lost the ballot are therefore a fair comparison, and in the first year the migrants' families had lower total income than they did.
Sources

Acosta, P., Calderón, C., Fajnzylber, P., & López, H. (2008). What is the impact of international remittances on poverty and inequality in Latin America? World Development, 36(1), 89–114. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.worlddev.2007.02.016

McKenzie, D., Gibson, J., & Stillman, S. (2007). Moving to opportunity, leaving behind what? Evaluating the initial effects of a migration policy on incomes and poverty in source areas. New Zealand Economic Papers, 41(2), 197–223. https://doi.org/10.1080/00779950709558509

Gibson, J., McKenzie, D., & Stillman, S. (2011). The impacts of international migration on remaining household members: Omnibus results from a migration lottery program. The Review of Economics and Statistics, 93(4), 1297–1318. https://doi.org/10.1162/REST_a_00129

Gibson, J., McKenzie, D., & Stillman, S. (2013). Accounting for selectivity and duration-dependent heterogeneity when estimating the impact of emigration on incomes and poverty in sending areas. Economic Development and Cultural Change, 61(2), 247–280. https://doi.org/10.1086/668276

When a son moves to Auckland and sends money home, the household gains the money and loses the son, meaning his wages, his work on the family plantation and his care for his parents. The simple method takes the household's income, subtracts the remittances, and calls the difference the gain from migration, which assumes that the son would have earned nothing if he had stayed.

Economists call the missing element the counterfactual, meaning what would have happened otherwise. Acosta and colleagues calculated the effect both ways for Latin America: when the migrant's lost earnings are ignored, migration reduces extreme poverty by about 14%, and when they are counted, the reduction is about 3%. For Mexico the direction reverses, so that once lost earnings are counted, migration is measured as increasing poverty (Acosta et al., 2008, Table 9).

The Tongan evidence is unusually strong, because New Zealand ran a ballot for Tongan migration and chance decided who left, so the families who lost the ballot are a fair comparison for the families of those who won. In the first year, the winners' families had lower total income, lower earnings, lower farm and business income and less food grown at home, and the remittances did not make up the loss (McKenzie, Gibson and Stillman, 2007). A later paper by the same authors on the Samoan ballot found the opposite result, poverty falling among the families left behind, with signs that the gain faded the longer the migrant had been away (Gibson, McKenzie and Stillman, 2013), so the answer differs by country and by how long the migrant has been away. Before crediting a remittance to a household, ask what the person who sent it would have earned, grown and cared for if they had stayed.

Part two · Tonga in the national accounts and in the household

The national accounts and the household account describe Tonga differently, and both rest on accurate figures

The national accounts show
  • Remittances equal about 39% of GDP: 38.6% in 2023 and 34.1% in 2024 on the National Reserve Bank of Tonga series, among the highest shares in the world.
  • Net aid equalled 20% of gross national income in 2023 and 51% in 2022, the year of the eruption.
  • Development assistance funded 51% of the national budget in 2023 to 2024.
  • Tonga is classed as upper middle income by income per person, and it has not been classed as a least developed country.
The household account shows
  • The person who earns the transfer is absent, and the household has lost their wages and the food they grew.
  • In rural Samoa, 29 dollars of every 100 received paid customary and church obligations before anything else; nobody has measured the Tongan share.
  • In the year to June 2025, Tonga paid 17.7 million US dollars to one creditor, out of 29.4 million in debt repayments, against an infrastructure budget of about 10.1 million.
  • On income per person Tonga would have lost its access to World Bank grants; it keeps them only through the exception the Bank makes for small island economies.
A claim for discussion

An income measure can record a gain in a country where a fuller account of the household records a loss.

The FAR-SIDS website: Tonga
Sources

National Reserve Bank of Tonga. (n.d.). Economic reviews: monthly economic update and remittances. Retrieved September 18, 2026, from https://www.reservebank.to/

World Bank. (n.d.). Net ODA received (% of GNI) (DT.ODA.ODAT.GN.ZS) [Data set]. World Development Indicators. Retrieved September 17, 2026, from https://data.worldbank.org/indicator/DT.ODA.ODAT.GN.ZS?locations=TO

New Zealand Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Trade. (2024). Tonga country plan 2024–27. https://www.mfat.govt.nz/assets/Aid-Prog-docs/4-year-plans/Tonga-Country-Plan-2024-27.pdf

World Bank. (n.d.). World Bank country and lending groups. World Bank Data Help Desk. Retrieved September 17, 2026, from https://datahelpdesk.worldbank.org/knowledgebase/articles/906519-world-bank-country-and-lending-groups

United Nations Conference on Trade and Development. (n.d.). UN list of least developed countries. Retrieved September 17, 2026, from https://unctad.org/topic/least-developed-countries/list

Agence France-Presse. (2026, April 5). Tonga’s debt to China hinders rebuild four years on from eruption. Kuwait Times. https://kuwaittimes.com/article/41949/business/tongas-debt-to-china-hinders-rebuild-four-years-on-from-eruption/

de Waegh, R. (2026). FAR-SIDS: Tonga. Islands and Small States Institute, University of Malta. https://roxydewaegh.github.io/FAR-SIDS/islands.html

On the screenOpen the Tonga page on the FAR-SIDS website and show the two flows over time.

Present this as a claim to argue with rather than as a settled fact. The left card shows what a ministry of finance or a donor reads. Remittances equal about 39% of GDP, 38.6% in 2023 and 34.1% in 2024 on the National Reserve Bank of Tonga series, among the highest shares in the world, net aid equalled a fifth of national income in 2023 and half of it in the year of the eruption, development assistance funded about half of the national budget, and Tonga is classed as upper middle income by income per person and has not been classed as a least developed country. On these figures, Tonga is one of the most supported small economies in the world.

The right card shows what parts one and two have added. The person who earns the transfer is absent, and the household has lost their wages and the food they grew. In rural Samoa, 29 dollars of every 100 received paid obligations before anything else, and nobody has measured the Tongan share. In the year to June 2025 Tonga paid 17.7 million US dollars to one creditor, out of 29.4 million in debt repayments, against an infrastructure budget of about 10.1 million. In addition, on income per person alone Tonga would have lost its access to World Bank grants, the money you saw in the IDA row this afternoon, and it keeps that access only through the exception the Bank makes for small island economies, a process called graduation that reading 1, the State of SIDS Report summary, sets out. The claim is that an income measure can record a gain in a country where a fuller account of the household records a loss. Invite the room to disagree, and note that the strongest objection is that the right card was selected to make the point, and a student who raises that objection should be given room to argue it.

Part three

From the national figure to the household, and what a ministry can do with what it finds

A national total records how much money arrived. The Sustainable Livelihoods Framework describes what that money meant for households, and your assignment asks you to apply it to your own island.

Why a total is not enough

What the money paid for, who in the house decided, and what the household had to survive.

The framework

Five assets, who controls each of them, and the conditions the household lives in.

What a ministry can do

The four tests a recommendation meets before it is worth writing.

A national total records how much money arrived, and the Sustainable Livelihoods Framework is the tool that describes what that money meant for the households that received it. Everything in this part is a tool you will use tomorrow and in your assignment, and I will introduce the framework through one worked example.

Part three · Why a framework is needed

A national total cannot show what the money paid for, who in the house decided, or what shock it had to cover

What it paid for

Which part of life did the money pay for?

A dollar spent on school fees, a dollar spent on a funeral and a dollar spent on a roof are the same dollar in the accounts and three different outcomes for a family.

Who decided

Who inside the house decided?

The money arrives with a person, that person's standing in the family shapes where it goes, and no account records who they were.

What it had to cover

What did the household have to survive?

After a cyclone, money that would have paid school fees pays for a roof. The household is no better off than before, although the figures may show more spending.

A national total cannot answer three questions that matter for a household. The first is which part of life the money paid for, because a dollar spent on school fees, a dollar spent on a funeral and a dollar spent on a roof are the same dollar in the accounts and three different outcomes for a family. The second is who inside the house decided, because the money arrives with a person, that person's standing in the family shapes where it goes, and no account records who they were.

The third is what the household had to survive. After a cyclone, a transfer that would have paid school fees pays for a roof, so the household is no better off than before, although the figures may show more spending. This question distinguishes the framework from a poverty line, because after a disaster a household can spend more than before and still be worse off, since it is replacing what it lost. Give an example of each question from Malta, so that the room sees that the questions apply beyond the Pacific. The three questions correspond to the three parts of the framework on the next two slides.

Part three · The framework, first part

The Sustainable Livelihoods Framework starts from the five assets a household uses to make a living

Human

Health, schooling and skills

These give a household its capacity to work.

Social

Networks, church, kin and the obligations that go with them

These are the people who help when a household cannot manage alone, and the standing that kavenga and misinale maintain.

Physical

House, boat, tools, road and water tank

These are the things the household owns and uses.

Financial

Cash, savings and credit

The transfer itself belongs here.

Natural

Land, reef, soil and water

These are what the island provides.

The frameworkA way of describing a household's life in three parts: the assets it has to work with, who controls each asset, and the conditions around them. The British aid ministry developed it in 1999 with these five assets (DFID, 1999). Natarajan and colleagues (2022), reading 3, keep only financial and physical assets at the centre and place two further parts beside them: relational power, meaning who controls each asset, and the climate and environment around the household. This module teaches all five assets, with those two parts added.
TomorrowEach of the five assets is a row of your map, with a column for remittances and a column for aid. In each cell you name the programme or channel through which that flow reaches the asset.
Sources

Department for International Development. (1999). Sustainable livelihoods guidance sheets. https://www.livelihoodscentre.org/documents/114097690/114438878/Sustainable+livelihoods+guidance+sheets.pdf

Natarajan, N., Newsham, A., Rigg, J., & Suhardiman, D. (2022). A sustainable livelihoods framework for the 21st century. World Development, 155, Article 105898. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.worlddev.2022.105898

The Sustainable Livelihoods Framework describes a household's life in three parts: what it has to work with, who controls each of those things, and the conditions around them. The framework calls the things a household works with capitals, and I will call them assets. The British aid ministry developed the framework in 1999 with these five assets, and the 2022 revision on your reading list, by Natarajan and colleagues, keeps only financial and physical assets at the centre and places two further parts beside them, relational power, meaning who controls each asset, and the climate and environment the household lives in. They drop the other three because they argue that calling health, kinship and land forms of capital accepts a market reading of a household’s life. This module teaches all five assets, because you need all five to see what a transfer touches, and it adds the two parts the 2022 paper proposes. Those two parts are the next slide.

Human assets are health, schooling and skills, meaning the capacity to work. Social assets are networks, church and kin, the people who help when you cannot manage alone, together with the obligations that keep a household in good standing with them, which is where kavenga and the misinale belong. Physical assets are the house, boat, tools, road and water tank. Financial assets are cash, savings and credit, including the transfer itself, and natural assets are land, reef, soil and water. Ask the room for one example of each from their own island before moving on. Tomorrow each of these five assets becomes a row of your map, with one column for remittances and one for aid, and in each cell you name the programme or channel through which that flow reaches the asset. In the Jamaica example you will see tomorrow, remittances reach everyday human and social life, where aid is weakest, and aid reaches roads and water, where remittances cannot, and that pattern follows from who decides each flow.

Part three · The framework, second and third parts

The framework then asks who controls each asset and under what conditions, and gender enters both questions

Who decides

Receiving and controlling differ

The question is who could spend the transfer without asking anyone, which is not always the person it was addressed to.

Who is left out

Aid selection also involves power

Across 8,062 donor appraisals, Pacific projects scored about 0.15 lower on the donors' six point scale, which Wood, Otor and Dornan (2022) attribute to distance and small size rather than to weak government.

Relational powerThe term Natarajan and colleagues (2022) use for who controls each asset. Class, gender, age, rank in the family and political connection decide who receives, who is chosen for a programme, who spends and who is left out. Ask it of both flows.
The conditions, in one exampleA cyclone destroys the house (physical), damages the land (natural), calls on church and kin (social), and forces the cash (financial) to replace what was lost. Who holds the money then decides whether what remains pays school fees (human) or a church obligation (social).
Sources

Natarajan, N., Newsham, A., Rigg, J., & Suhardiman, D. (2022). A sustainable livelihoods framework for the 21st century. World Development, 155, Article 105898. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.worlddev.2022.105898

Department of Employment and Workplace Relations. (2026). PALM scheme data publication, June 2026 [Data set]. Pacific Australia Labour Mobility scheme. https://www.palmscheme.gov.au/

Bank of Jamaica. (2011). Remittances to Jamaica: Findings from a national survey of remittance recipients. https://www.boj.org.jm/uploads/pdf/papers_pamphlets/papers_pamphlets_Remittances_to_Jamaica_-_Findings_from_a_National_Survey_of_Remittance_Recipients.pdf

Wood, T., Otor, S., & Dornan, M. (2022). Why are aid projects less effective in the Pacific? Development Policy Review, 40(3), Article e12573. https://doi.org/10.1111/dpr.12573

The second part of the framework asks who controls each asset, which Natarajan and colleagues call relational power: class, gender, age, rank in the family and political connection decide who receives, who is chosen for a programme, who spends and who is left out, and the question applies to both flows. Gender is a question inside every part of the framework rather than a separate part, and it takes four concrete forms here. Of the 3,715 Tongans on PALM visas in June 2026, 3,095 were men, because the fruit picking corridors recruit men, while care and nursing corridors recruit more women, so the type of work decides who is absent from the household. In Jamaica's national survey of 2,072 remittance recipients, three in four were women (Bank of Jamaica, 2011), and that survey dates from 2010, so a Jamaican student can record that the latest national evidence on who receives is fifteen years old. Receiving and controlling also differ, so the useful question is who could spend the transfer without asking anyone, rather than to whom it was addressed. On the aid side, donors score their own projects, and across 8,062 appraisals Pacific projects scored about 0.15 lower on the donors' six point scale, which is the scale a donor uses to rate its own project from failure to full success, because the islands are distant and small rather than badly governed (Wood, Otor and Dornan, 2022), so being hard to reach is itself a disadvantage in who is chosen.

The third part is the conditions around all of this, and one example shows how they work. A cyclone destroys the house, which is a physical asset, damages the land, which is natural, calls on church and kin, which are social, and forces the cash, which is financial, to replace what was lost. Who holds the money then decides whether what remains pays school fees, a human asset, or a church obligation, a social one, so a single transfer touches all five assets, and who controls the money decides where it goes. Natarajan and colleagues call these two parts relational power and the climate and environment context, and they place them beside the assets rather than underneath them.

Part three · The indicators ministries publish

The indicators your ministry already publishes cannot show who received the money or who decided how to spend it

GDP per person

Output divided by population

It counts the transfer when it arrives, and it does not count the migrant's lost wages.

Poverty headcount

Share of people below a poverty line

A remittance that lifts one household just over the line and does nothing for another shows as a single change.

Human Development Index

Income, schooling and life expectancy combined

It records nothing on who inside the household received anything.

Multidimensional Poverty Index

Ten deprivations in health, education and living standards

It comes closer to the assets, and it still records neither obligation payments nor who decides.

Food Insecurity Experience Scale

Eight questions on running short of food

It records how severe the shortage was. The Kingston study used a scale of the same kind and found the effect of remittances there.

Gini coefficient

Inequality across households in one number

It cannot distinguish a country where remittances reach the poor from one where they reach the middle.

An indicatorOne measure published for every country every year. These six are the indicators most small island governments report, and each measures something well. None was designed to show a transfer arriving with a person.
Question three of the assignmentWhich indicators should the ministry monitor, and why do the ones it uses now fail to answer the question? This list is the starting point for your argument.
Sources

World Bank. (n.d.). GDP per capita (current US$) (NY.GDP.PCAP.CD) [Data set]. World Development Indicators. Retrieved September 17, 2026, from https://data.worldbank.org/indicator/NY.GDP.PCAP.CD

World Bank. (n.d.). Poverty headcount ratio at national poverty lines (% of population) (SI.POV.NAHC) [Data set]. World Development Indicators. Retrieved September 17, 2026, from https://data.worldbank.org/indicator/SI.POV.NAHC

World Bank. (n.d.). Gini index (SI.POV.GINI) [Data set]. World Development Indicators. Retrieved September 17, 2026, from https://data.worldbank.org/indicator/SI.POV.GINI

United Nations Development Programme. (n.d.). Human Development Index. Human Development Reports. Retrieved September 17, 2026, from https://hdr.undp.org/data-center/human-development-index

Oxford Poverty and Human Development Initiative & United Nations Development Programme. (2025). Global multidimensional poverty index 2025: Overlapping hardships, poverty and climate hazards. https://ophi.org.uk/global-mpi

Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations. (n.d.). Food Insecurity Experience Scale. Retrieved September 17, 2026, from https://www.fao.org/in-action/voices-of-the-hungry/fies/en/

Thomas-Hope, E. (2025). Migrant remittances, food security and inclusive social development in Jamaica. In J. Crush, A. Chikanda, & S. Ramachandran (Eds.), New directions in South-South migration (pp. 63–82). Springer. https://doi.org/10.1007/978-981-97-9715-8_4

Question three of your assignment asks which indicators the ministry should monitor and why the ones it uses now do not answer the question. These six are the ones most small island governments publish. GDP per person, which is output divided by population, counts the transfer when it arrives and does not count the migrant's lost wages at all. The poverty headcount, the share of people below a poverty line, shows a remittance that lifts one household just over the line and does nothing for another as a single change. The Human Development Index combines income, schooling and life expectancy into one number a year and records nothing on who inside the household received anything. The Multidimensional Poverty Index counts ten deprivations across health, education and living standards, so it comes closer to the assets, and it still records neither obligation payments nor who decides.

The Food Insecurity Experience Scale asks eight questions on whether the household ran short of food and records how severe the shortage was. In Kingston, Thomas-Hope (2025) asked the questions of a scale of the same kind, the Household Food Insecurity Access Scale, and found that households receiving remittances were no less likely to run short of food, while among poor households the shortage was less severe, so a measure that recorded only yes or no would have reported no effect where there was one. Finally, the Gini coefficient expresses inequality across households in one number, and it cannot distinguish a country where remittances reach the poor from one where they reach the middle. Each of these indicators measures something well, and none was designed to show a transfer arriving with a person, so in question three you argue which of them your own ministry should keep, which it should add to, and why.

Part three · A recommendation a ministry can act on

A recommendation that a ministry can act on meets four tests, and the assignment is marked against them

  1. An existing instrument to deliver it, such as a household survey already in the field or a ministry that already publishes the figure.
  2. A cost the budget can bear, stated against the fiscal position you described in your first question.
  3. A question the government is already asking, so that somebody wants the answer.
  4. A plain statement of what it will not do. A change in measurement does not change how much money arrives.
The Jamaica model answer on the VLE

About fifteen questions added to a survey already in the field

Add about fifteen questions on remittances to the Survey of Living Conditions, which the statistics office already runs: cash, goods and bills paid separately, who receives, how regularly, and what leaves the household again. The questions are cheap to add, and they answer a question the government asked after Hurricane Melissa, namely which households already have a private safety net.

The standard

Make one recommendation and argue it against all four tests, because five recommendations cannot each be argued properly in the space you have.

Question four of your assignment asks for one recommendation, argued against four tests. The recommendation needs an existing instrument to deliver it, such as a household survey already in the field or a ministry that already publishes the figure. It needs a cost the budget can bear, stated against the fiscal position you described in question one, and it needs to answer a question the government is already asking, so that somebody wants the answer. Finally, it needs a plain statement of what it will not do.

The Jamaica model answer on the VLE proposes one change in measurement: about fifteen questions added to the Survey of Living Conditions, which the statistics office already runs. The questions ask about cash, goods and bills paid separately, following the lesson of the Tongan surveys, about who receives, about how regularly the money comes, because a regular flow can fund a business, and about what leaves the household again as church and community giving. The change is cheap, it uses an instrument already in the field, and it answers a question the Jamaican government asked after Hurricane Melissa, namely which households already have a private safety net. Its last paragraph states that it will not change how much money arrives. Make one recommendation and argue it well, because five recommendations cannot each be argued against four tests in the space the assignment gives you.

Block two · A completed example

The Jamaica model answer shows the level of detail expected in each cell, and it records what the writer could not find

Human assets, remittances

School fees, uniforms, books and lunch money

Relatives send this money monthly and often earmark it, and they also pay private health costs when the public system cannot cope. The writer names a cousin's exam fees paid from Florida as her own experience.

Human assets, aid

PATH, and education loans

PATH, the government's conditional cash transfer, pays a benefit tied to school attendance and clinic visits and is supported by World Bank lending. The Inter-American Development Bank lends for education. Both were found on the lenders' project pages.

What the writer could not find

Recorded as findings

The latest national figure for households receiving remittances, 43%, dates from 2008. The only national evidence that women are three quarters of recipients dates from 2010. Nobody has yet asked whether households receiving remittances recovered faster from Hurricane Melissa.

A map that records where the group looked and what it could not find scores higher than a map that fills every cell with a guess.
